issues.subcategory: Contradictory replication sample sizes
issues.description: The manuscript states that all included studies met a CREP minimum sample size of 120, but later reports that included sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374, and Table 1 lists six of seven replications with N below 120. This contradiction matters because sample-size eligibility, power, and inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis are unclear.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.subcategory: Sample-size range conflicts with stated minimum
issues.description: The reported sample-size range includes values below the stated minimum of 120. This undermines confidence in the reported inclusion rules and in claims that the replication studies were adequately powered according to CREP criteria.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: Underpowered replications despite power claim
issues.description: The manuscript claims the minimum N of 120 ensured adequate statistical power, yet most included studies had N values of 80–116. For effects around r = .15–.30, many individual replications would have low-to-moderate power, especially for the smaller effects. This affects interpretation of nonsignificant individual studies and replication success/failure judgments.
issues.quote: collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.subcategory: Incorrect sign of effect-size differences
issues.description: Table 3 appears to compute or label effect-size differences inconsistently. For example, BYU-Sp16 advantageous has replication r = -0.02 and original r = -0.33; replication minus original equals +0.31, not -0.31. Conversely, original minus replication equals -0.31, but other textual interpretations describe replication effects as smaller. The sign convention is not clearly defined and appears reversed relative to the table labels, which can lead to incorrect conclusions about whether replications are larger or smaller than the original.

issues.subcategory: Misinterpretation of effect-size difference direction
issues.description: The authors state that five connection effects were significantly smaller than the original. However, most replication effects are positive while the original is negative; they are not simply 'smaller' in magnitude, but opposite in direction. In Table 3, the difference values are negative because of an apparent original-minus-replication calculation, not because replication effects are smaller in the ordinary signed sense. This obscures the substantive interpretation.
issues.quote: five of the seven replications had effect sizes significantly smaller from the original study, as evidenced by 95% CIs for the difference in effect sizes that did not include zero.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect or inconsistent prediction interval reporting
issues.description: Prediction intervals are reported inconsistently across the manuscript. In the results, the self-disclosure safety PI is [-.54, -.03], but in the discussion it is reported as [-.40, -.15], which is the confidence interval from the results, not the prediction interval. This matters because prediction intervals are used to draw conclusions about future-study effects.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was -.28, 95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03], p < .001.

issues.subcategory: Discussion misreports safety prediction interval
issues.description: The discussion reports the 95% PI for safety as [-.40, -.15], conflicting with the results section's PI of [-.54, -.03]. The discussion value appears to be the confidence interval, not the prediction interval, leading to overconfident claims about future studies.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.subcategory: Discussion misreports connection prediction interval and significance
issues.description: The results section reports the connection meta-analytic effect as r = .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065, which is not statistically significant at .05. The discussion says the meta-analytic effect was significantly different from zero and reports a different PI of [-.07, .27]. This is a direct contradiction affecting the interpretation of a central finding.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero. We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number discrepancy for expression
issues.description: The results report an FSN of 3 studies for opportunity to express self, but the discussion states that five unreported studies would reduce the meta-analytic p-value to nonsignificance. This inconsistency undermines the reported robustness assessment.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies.

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number discrepancy for expression in discussion
issues.description: The discussion contradicts the results section by stating that the fail-safe number for expression was five, not three. The robustness interpretation is therefore unclear.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number discrepancy for connection
issues.description: The results report an FSN of 5 studies for connection, while the discussion reports 11 studies. This changes the apparent stability of the result and indicates reporting or calculation errors.
issues.quote: The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number discrepancy for connection in discussion
issues.description: The discussion contradicts the results section by reporting an FSN of 11 for connection, rather than 5. This affects claims about instability of the finding.
issues.quote: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.subcategory: Use of fail-safe N with nonsignificant meta-analytic result
issues.description: Fail-safe N is described as identifying the number of nonsignificant unpublished studies needed to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to nonsignificance. Yet it is reported for the connection outcome where p = .065, already nonsignificant. The interpretation of an FSN in that setting is unclear and potentially inappropriate.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate confidence in FSN/file-drawer interpretation
issues.description: The authors use low or high fail-safe numbers as evidence for future replication stability, but fail-safe N is a limited and often discouraged indicator of publication bias/robustness. It assumes hypothetical null studies and does not account for small-study effects, selection mechanisms, or heterogeneity. With only seven known CREP replications and preregistration, file-drawer assumptions are also unclear.
issues.quote: These results also seemed to be somewhat robust, as indicated by a high FSN (133).

issues.subcategory: Publication bias inferred from replication-original difference without formal test
issues.description: The manuscript interprets smaller replication effect sizes and prediction intervals as indicating publication bias in the original study. A single original study cannot establish publication bias, and differences could arise from sampling error, historical changes in Facebook use, procedural deviations, or population differences. This is an overinterpretation of meta-analytic results.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study.

issues.subcategory: Prediction interval overinterpretation
issues.description: The authors state that a 95% PI shows that 95% of future studies would find an effect in the interval. Prediction intervals estimate the distribution of true effects for comparable future studies under the fitted random-effects model; they do not guarantee that 95% of observed future study estimates will fall there, especially with only seven studies and uncertain heterogeneity.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study’s

issues.subcategory: Meta-analysis of correlations using raw r rather than Fisher z not justified
issues.description: The methods state that the rma function accepted effect size r and N parameters, suggesting correlations were meta-analyzed on the r scale. Standard practice is to transform correlations to Fisher's z for analysis and back-transform estimates, because the sampling variance of r is nonnormal and depends on the true correlation. Without clarification, the meta-analytic estimates, CIs, and heterogeneity statistics may be biased or incorrectly estimated.
issues.quote: The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters

issues.subcategory: Incorrect equivalence of beta and r not generally valid
issues.description: The note claims effect size r is equivalent to standardized beta. This is only true in simple linear regression with a single predictor and identical handling of variables. If any regressions included covariates, missing-data differences, or nonstandard scoring, the equivalence would not hold. The manuscript does not sufficiently establish that every original and replication analysis was exactly a single-predictor regression.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: Original effect-size extraction unclear for missing beta
issues.description: The original study did not report a beta coefficient for the expression outcome, but the meta-analysis uses an original r of .15 in Table 3. The manuscript does not report the original t statistic, degrees of freedom, or exact calculation used to derive that value. This limits auditability of the original-replication comparison.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.

issues.subcategory: Original advantageous effect size inconsistent
issues.description: The abstract and results text refer to the original advantageous effect size as -.30, whereas Table 3 uses -.33. The discussion also says '-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33'. This inconsistency affects comparisons between original and replication effects.
issues.quote: Self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)

issues.subcategory: Original advantageous effect-size inconsistency in table
issues.description: Table 3 lists the original advantageous r as -.33, conflicting with the abstract and Table 1 beta of -.300. The manuscript does not explain whether -.33 was derived from t/df while -.30 is standardized beta, or why different values are used.

issues.subcategory: P-value/beta/N inconsistencies in Table 1
issues.description: Several p-values appear inconsistent with the listed standardized beta values and sample sizes for simple regression/correlation. For example, with N = 80 and beta/r = -.209, a two-tailed test would generally yield p around .06–.07, depending on exact df, close but not necessarily matching; with N = 90 and r = -.205, p near .05 is plausible. Because the manuscript relies on beta as r, the exact df and missing-data Ns for each outcome should be reported. Without outcome-specific Ns, readers cannot verify p-values.

issues.subcategory: Non-identical direct replications
issues.description: The manuscript characterizes all studies as direct replications, but reports multiple procedural deviations: lab versus online administration, individual versus group administration, wording differences, item-order differences, and 4-point versus 5-point self-esteem scales. These deviations may affect responses and comparability, especially because moderators were not analyzed.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods). Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: Measurement deviations in Rosenberg scale
issues.description: One replication changed item order and wording on four of ten RSE items, including a wording difference that changes nuance by removing 'At times'. Two replications used a 5-point instead of 4-point response scale. These changes can alter scale distributions, reliability, and associations with outcomes, compromising direct comparability.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., ‘At times I think I am no good at all’ vs. ‘I think I am no good at all’), and (b) most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.subcategory: Self-esteem scale response-format inconsistency
issues.description: Using different response scales for the same self-esteem construct across sites may change the operationalization and distribution of self-esteem. Although correlations are scale-invariant under linear transformations, response-format changes can alter reliability, response styles, and range restriction, which matters for cross-study comparability.
issues.quote: the 10-item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSE; Rosenberg, 1965) which assesses global self-esteem on a scale of 1 to 4 (1 to 5 in two of the studies).

issues.subcategory: Facebook perceptions vs actual behavior
issues.description: The manuscript at times discusses Facebook benefits, use, self-disclosure tendencies, and social compensation as though the study measured actual behavior or benefits. However, the outcomes are self-reported perceptions of Facebook relative to face-to-face interactions. This mismatch limits conclusions about real self-disclosure behavior or social outcomes.
issues.quote: This replication meta-analysis explored the robustness of a highly cited study showing that those with low self-esteem perceived benefits for self-disclosure through Facebook compared to face-to-face interactions

issues.subcategory: Comparative FTF versus Facebook items confound platform preference and trait perception
issues.description: Safety and advantages are measured as perceptions of Facebook compared to face-to-face interactions. Such comparative ratings may reflect fear of FTF interactions, social anxiety, general negativity, Facebook familiarity, or current platform use rather than perceived Facebook-specific affordances. The design does not disentangle these constructs.
issues.quote: Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF.

issues.subcategory: Causal wording from correlational design
issues.description: The study uses regression/correlation with self-esteem predicting perceptions at a single time point. Phrases such as 'self-esteem predicts' and discussion of Facebook mitigating anxiety may imply causal direction, but the design cannot establish that self-esteem causes differences in Facebook perceptions.
issues.quote: lower self-esteem was a significant predictor of perceiving Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose than FTF.

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confounding variables
issues.description: The analyses appear to use only self-esteem as a predictor. Potential confounds such as social anxiety, depression, extraversion, actual Facebook use intensity, number of friends, prior negative social experiences, gender, age, and platform preference could explain the observed associations. This limits causal and theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables

issues.subcategory: Missing missing-data handling details
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that some studies did not document missing-data handling, exclusions, or composite calculations. This is a serious reproducibility issue because correlations and Ns can vary depending on listwise versus pairwise deletion, exclusion rules, and scale scoring.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: No systematic missing-data reporting
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the amount or pattern of missing data by study or outcome, nor how missing responses were handled. In a multi-site meta-analysis, differences in missing-data rules can affect study-specific effect sizes and weights.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: Outcome-specific Ns not reported
issues.description: Table 1 reports a single N per study, but if missing data differed across variables, the regression Ns could differ by outcome. Because effect sizes and p-values depend on outcome-specific degrees of freedom, the absence of outcome-specific Ns limits verification and replication.
issues.quote: Study | Authors | Authors | N | β | p

issues.subcategory: Incomplete demographic information
issues.description: Race/ethnicity was collected in only three replications and no other demographics were collected in the remaining studies. This limits assessment of sample comparability, representativeness, and potential moderators of replication differences.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected

issues.subcategory: Table 2 omitted from manuscript text provided
issues.description: The manuscript refers to Table 2 for demographic and descriptive statistics, but the table content is absent except for a note. Without descriptive statistics, readers cannot assess scale distributions, range restriction, site differences, or comparability to the original study.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study’s descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.subcategory: Analysis scripts not uniformly available
issues.description: Only two studies included analysis scripts, and scoring for some studies had to be inferred from means. This makes the replication meta-analysis difficult to audit and raises the possibility of inconsistent scoring across sites.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent composite scoring across studies
issues.description: The manuscript indicates that most studies apparently used mean-averaged scores, whereas the Gordon study appeared to sum items. Although linear transformations do not affect correlations if applied consistently within a scale, inconsistent scoring can affect descriptive comparability, reliability reporting, and any analyses not purely correlation-based. It also indicates lack of standardized analytic procedures.
issues.quote: The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: Meta-analysis inclusion criteria insufficiently specified
issues.description: The manuscript states that 17 OSF forks existed and seven studies met criteria, but does not fully account for the other 10 forks: whether they collected data, failed to reach N, lacked posted data, had null or incomplete results, or were excluded for other reasons. This creates potential selection bias in the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks” representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository. All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous preregistration content
issues.description: The manuscript says data collection and analysis methods were preregistered at each study's OSF page, but does not specify whether the meta-analysis protocol itself was preregistered, including inclusion criteria, effect-size extraction, model choice, handling of deviations, and outcomes. This leaves researcher degrees of freedom in the synthesis.
issues.quote: the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page

issues.subcategory: Post hoc model-selection rationale
issues.description: The authors compared REML and DL estimators and selected REML because it produced 'more interpretable' heterogeneity estimates. Without a prespecified criterion, choosing between estimators after seeing results introduces analytic flexibility, especially with only seven studies where heterogeneity estimates are unstable.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneity inference with very small k
issues.description: Although limitations acknowledge small-k bias, the results still interpret Q, T2, and I2 as evidence of limited or little heterogeneity. With only seven studies, Q has low power and I2 intervals are very wide; saying there is little evidence of heterogeneity can be misleading.
issues.quote: The variance measures showed little evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 5.81, p = 0.445; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 6.08%, 95% CI [0%, 79.94%].

issues.subcategory: Overreliance on individual-study significance
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly judges consistency with the original by whether individual replications are statistically significant. Replication evaluation based on dichotomous p-values is low-powered and can misclassify studies, especially when effect sizes are similar but nonsignificant. The authors do report effect sizes, but interpretive language still emphasizes significance counts.
issues.quote: Four of the seven replication studies were consistent with the original study, showing self-esteem to be a significant predictor

issues.subcategory: Questionable claim that p = .05 supports true null likelihood
issues.description: The manuscript states that p-values between .04 and .05 are relatively more likely under a true null than a false one. This statement depends on assumptions about alternative distributions and p-curve logic, and it is not generally valid as presented. It risks overinterpreting the original p = .05 finding as evidence for the null.
issues.quote: p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: Incorrect significant/non-significant interpretation for expression
issues.description: For opportunity to express self, the meta-analytic effect is reported as r = .08, p = .021, with 95% CI/PI apparently excluding zero, yet the manuscript concludes that the result supports 'no relationship' because individual regressions were nonsignificant. This conflates individual-study power with meta-analytic evidence and creates an inconsistent interpretation.
issues.quote: Even though the effect size meta-analysis revealed that the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero... all individual replications found regression coefficients not significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: Abstract says expression CIs all include zero despite meta-analysis p = .021
issues.description: The abstract states that all 95% CIs for effect sizes included zero for expression, but the results report a statistically significant meta-analytic effect and a CI/PI between .01 and .14. If the abstract refers only to individual-study CIs, this is ambiguous and omits the contradictory meta-analytic finding.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).

issues.subcategory: Possible incorrect confidence interval terminology for expression
issues.description: The results state 'the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14'. A CI and PI are distinct intervals and generally should not have the same bounds; the exact CI is not explicitly reported. This makes it unclear whether .01–.14 is a CI, PI, or both.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.subcategory: Prediction interval implausibly narrow when tau2 estimated zero
issues.description: For outcomes with T2 = 0, the manuscript reports narrow prediction intervals nearly identical to confidence intervals. With only seven studies, uncertainty in tau2 should make prediction intervals wider; some software methods that ignore tau2 uncertainty can understate uncertainty. This should be noted, especially since conclusions about future studies rely on PIs.

issues.subcategory: No control for administration mode
issues.description: Administration mode varied across studies, including lab, online, and mixed administration, but was not modeled or controlled. Mode could influence disclosure-related responses due to privacy, context, perceived anonymity, or demand characteristics, threatening internal comparability.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods).

issues.subcategory: Group administration may compromise privacy
issues.description: The SAU replication ran participants in groups of two to six, unlike other lab studies where participants completed questionnaires alone. Because the constructs involve self-esteem and disclosure perceptions, reduced privacy or peer presence could influence responses.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: No assessment of current Facebook use or eligibility
issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether participants were required to be current Facebook users, how frequently they used Facebook, or whether non-users were excluded. Perceptions of Facebook self-disclosure and connection are difficult to interpret for participants who rarely use or do not use Facebook.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers

issues.subcategory: Changing social media ecology threatens construct stability
issues.description: The study replicates a 2012 Facebook study in 2016–2017, when Facebook's role among undergraduates may have changed substantially. The manuscript discusses this post hoc, but the design does not measure alternative-platform use sufficiently to test whether Facebook perceptions reflect broader social media preferences rather than the original construct.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others

issues.subcategory: Restricted undergraduate US samples
issues.description: All replication participants were undergraduates at five US institutions. Claims about Facebook users, individuals with low self-esteem, or social compensation generally may not generalize to older adults, nonstudents, non-US users, or users in different cultural and platform contexts.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralization to Facebook users broadly
issues.description: The introduction frames Facebook as a global platform with two billion users, but the empirical sample is US undergraduates. This framing risks overgeneralizing findings from a narrow population to global Facebook users.
issues.quote: Facebook is a dominant platform that affects the thinking, emotions, behavior, and interactions of its active users, some two billion people worldwide

issues.subcategory: Institutional diversity overstated
issues.description: The manuscript emphasizes diverse institutions, but the sample remains limited to five U.S. colleges/universities and undergraduate psychology participant pools. Institutional variety does not solve demographic, cultural, and age restrictions.
issues.quote: These CREP research teams represented five diverse institutions, both public and private, in urban and suburban settings in the eastern and western U.S.

issues.subcategory: Weak test of social compensation theory
issues.description: The study measures perceptions of Facebook affordances, not actual compensatory use, anxiety reduction, social skill deficits, social outcomes, or longitudinal compensation. Therefore, support for social compensation theory is indirect and limited.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory

issues.subcategory: Theory claim inconsistent with mixed/null findings
issues.description: Social compensation theory is invoked even though the connection and expression outcomes—central to compensation—were weak, inconsistent, or opposite in direction. The theory discussion should be more constrained to disclosure safety/advantages perceptions.
issues.quote: This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.subcategory: Speculative cultural explanation unsupported by data
issues.description: The discussion proposes cultural individualism/collectivism explanations for differences with Turkish university students, but the present study did not measure culture or cross-cultural samples. This is speculative and should not be presented as a substantive explanation without data.
issues.quote: It is also possible that more collectivist cultures, like Turkey... may prompt people to use Facebook for different reasons than those in individualist cultures.

issues.subcategory: Speculative platform-shift explanation untested
issues.description: The discussion suggests that changes in use of Instagram and Snapchat may explain replication differences, but alternative platform use was apparently not measured. This is plausible but untested, and should be clearly labeled as speculation.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram

issues.subcategory: No details on recruitment, incentives, or exclusion criteria
issues.description: The methods do not provide site-specific recruitment procedures, compensation/credit, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, or whether participants completed the study more than once. These details are needed to evaluate sampling bias and replicate the studies.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.subcategory: No IRB/consent procedural details beyond general approval
issues.description: Although the CREP approval process required evidence of IRB approval, the manuscript does not report site-specific ethical approvals or consent procedures in enough detail to evaluate whether procedures were uniform across sites.
issues.quote: compiled evidence of their ability to conduct the study (completed study materials, a video of the experimental procedure, and evidence of institutional review board approval).

issues.subcategory: No item examples or full scale content in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript describes the Facebook perception subscales but does not provide item examples or the exact wording, response anchors, or scoring rules in the manuscript. Although materials are on OSF, basic measurement details are needed for evaluation without external files.
issues.quote: Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others.

issues.subcategory: Low reliability for connection in some samples
issues.description: The connection subscale reliability was as low as alpha = .68. This level may attenuate associations and contribute to replication variability, especially with only three items. The implications of measurement error for effect-size comparisons are not addressed.
issues.quote: connection: .68 to .84

issues.subcategory: No correction or framework for multiple outcomes
issues.description: The study tests four related outcomes and multiple replication-original comparisons without discussing multiplicity or a clear confirmatory hierarchy. Although replication studies may target prespecified outcomes, interpretation of individual p-values and significant meta-analytic effects should consider multiple testing.
issues.quote: For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions.

issues.subcategory: Direct-Plus additions may create uncontrolled context effects
issues.description: Three studies included additional personality measures after the focal measures. Although administered after the primary measures, knowing the study includes additional measures could affect session length, participant expectations, or exclusion/missingness. The manuscript does not report which sites had these measures or test whether they differed.
issues.quote: Three studies were Direct-Plus replications that included measures of personality, presented after participants completed self-esteem and Facebook perception measures

issues.subcategory: CREP acronym inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between Collaborative Replication and Education Project and Collaborative Research and Education Project. This is minor but indicates inconsistent reporting.
issues.quote: several research teams at U.S. colleges and universities replicated the study as part of the Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP; Grahe, et al., 2016; https://osf.io/wfc6u/).

issues.subcategory: Meta-analytic advantageous original effect conflicts across sections
issues.description: The discussion states the original advantageous effect as -.33 while the abstract states -.30 and results section says 'vs. -.30'. This inconsistency affects narrative conclusions about shrinkage from original to replication.
issues.quote: All of the replications showed effects in the same direction as the original, but with widely varying and smaller effect sizes than the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous use of p = .050 as significant original finding
issues.description: The manuscript treats the original connection p-value of .050 as significant. Depending on rounding and criterion, p = .050 exactly is borderline; if rounded from >.050 it would not meet p < .05. This matters because the connection outcome is classified as an original positive finding to be replicated.
issues.quote: Original | Forest & Wood | Forest & Wood | 80 | n/a* | .181 |  | -.220 | .050

issues.subcategory: No reporting of original study comparability details
issues.description: The manuscript notes the original did not specify lab versus online administration, but does not provide a systematic comparison of original and replication procedures, recruitment, eligibility, item wording, or timing. This limits evaluation of whether failures to replicate reflect effect instability or procedural mismatch.
issues.quote: As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online, researchers employed both methods

issues.subcategory: No blinding relevance or demand-characteristic assessment
issues.description: Although this is a questionnaire study, no information is provided on whether experimenters were aware of hypotheses, whether participants were aware they were in a replication, or whether demand characteristics were minimized. This is especially relevant in undergraduate replication projects with student experimenters.
issues.quote: Contributors and their faculty mentors... compiled evidence of their ability to conduct the study

issues.subcategory: Weights and variance inputs not reported
issues.description: The forest plots are said to include weights, but the manuscript text does not report weights or the exact sampling variance formula. For correlation meta-analysis, variance specification is essential for reproducibility, particularly if raw r rather than Fisher z was used.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Forest plot for meta-analysis of CREP replication studies showing effect sizes, weights, and 95% confidence intervals.

issues.subcategory: Table formatting duplicates columns and labels
issues.description: Tables 1 and 3 contain duplicated 'Authors' columns and repeated outcome labels/CI columns. This creates ambiguity in reading values and may indicate transcription or formatting errors in reported data.
issues.quote: Study | Authors | Authors | N | β | p

issues.subcategory: No exact meta-analytic CIs for all outcomes in text
issues.description: For some outcomes, CIs are reported, but for expression the exact meta-analytic CI is not separately stated and is conflated with the prediction interval. Complete reporting of effect estimate, SE, CI, PI, tau2, and model details for each outcome is needed.
issues.quote: r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero, and the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.subcategory: No robust small-sample adjustment for random-effects meta-analysis
issues.description: With only seven studies per meta-analysis, conventional normal-approximation REML CIs can be anti-conservative. Methods such as Knapp-Hartung adjustments are often recommended for random-effects meta-analyses with small k. The manuscript does not mention using or considering them.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML

issues.subcategory: Temporal generalizability overclaim
issues.description: The manuscript concludes future researchers can be confident about Facebook-related effects despite rapid changes in platform use and a replication period several years after the original. The conclusions do not sufficiently condition generalizability on time period and user cohort.
issues.quote: future researchers can be relatively confident of finding that low self-esteem predicts perceptions that Facebook is a safer and more advantageous place to self-disclose than FTF interactions.

issues.subcategory: Social connection outcome not equivalent to acquaintance-related Facebook functions
issues.description: The discussion compares the study's 'opportunity to connect' and 'expression' perception measures to another study's acquaintance-related Facebook functions. These may not measure the same construct, making the theoretical comparison potentially invalid.
issues.quote: using Facebook for acquaintance-related functions (e.g., being known by others and meeting new people), suggesting that those lower in self-esteem used Facebook for connection and expression. This finding runs contrary to the results of our meta-analysis

issues.subcategory: Unsupported 'considerable' effect-size characterization
issues.description: The safety meta-analytic effect r = -.28 is described as 'considerable' without benchmark justification or practical significance analysis. This may overstate the magnitude, especially given heterogeneity and self-report measures.
issues.quote: the size of this effect is considerable.

issues.subcategory: No participant nesting/site-level dependency modeling beyond study-level meta-analysis
issues.description: The synthesis uses study-level effects but does not consider individual participant data meta-analysis or site-level covariates, despite data availability. This is not inherently wrong, but limits ability to handle differing measurement formats, demographics, missing data, or administration modes consistently.
issues.quote: One replication study failed to report regression results, so we calculated the regression statistics from the study’s dataset which was made openly available on OSF.

issues.subcategory: No explanation of why one study failed to report regression results
issues.description: A replication lacked reported regression results, requiring reanalysis by the meta-analytic authors. The manuscript does not identify which study, whether the reanalysis matched preregistered analyses, or whether other study results were independently verified from raw data.
issues.quote: One replication study failed to report regression results, so we calculated the regression statistics from the study’s dataset

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent data storage and item-level availability
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that individual item-level data were not always stored. This prevents checking reliability, reverse scoring, exclusions, and measurement equivalence across sites.
issues.quote: Data were not always collected or stored consistently (e.g., race collected in some but not all studies; individual item-level data were not always stored).

issues.subcategory: No moderator analyses despite known procedural heterogeneity
issues.description: The authors identify known procedural differences but do not analyze moderators, citing small numbers. While understandable, this means the pooled estimates combine potentially non-equivalent studies and cannot determine whether deviations explain heterogeneity or nonreplication.
issues.quote: Because each of these potential moderating factors occurred in only one or two of the seven replications, we chose not to explore these issues in more depth.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between regression terminology and bivariate effect sizes
issues.description: The manuscript describes 'regression results' but apparently uses bivariate standardized betas/correlations. If the original study included multiple regression or covariates, extracting comparable bivariate r values from t statistics would require partial correlations, not zero-order correlations. The exact model specification is not fully stated.
issues.quote: The original Forest and Wood (2012) regression results included t-statistics and degrees of freedom for all variables, so we chose to calculate effect size r for all four outcome variables in the study.
